What, Carla thought, has happened to all of us?

Thousands of houses in millions of acres of forests are lost every year to fire. What's happening now is that urban growth and climate change are teaming up to make wildfires more complicated, and much more destructive, than they used to be. In the 1990s there were about forty thousand housing units a year in the so-called wildland-urban interface, the strip of forest next to a town like Pine Hollow. Recently the addition rate is closer to 180,000. Migrating retirees and people looking for (they think) peaceful and affordable scenic surroundings have built a half million new houses in the western forest in the past ten years. A few years back Kristine Maffei at the University of Wisconsin-Madison modeled the Lodgepole Complex Fire that burned 350,000 acres in the Yukon Flats in 2007. She compared wildfires that started in dense lodgepole forest and wildfires that burned in sparse black spruce forest. The forest with fewer trees and less fuel was twice as likely to get to the edge of the spruce forest and burn down every house on its far side.

Spruce species have needle-shaped leaves that can retain moisture and burn only at high temperatures. Lodgepole pines have live foliage—lots of it—with a fast ignition and a low flash point. There's a concentration effect: a tree like a lodgepole sprays flaming sap and resin for up to twenty-five feet. Fire jewels, the firefighters call them. The difference was a one-point change in the Keetch-Byram Drought Index.

It's not enough anymore to say (and it wasn't always true) that the first people to build close to the forest in Sage Hill didn't know as much as they did later. Or that they had a different idea of what a community was, or that a lot of people didn't have the same options other people had, or that the sums of the individual decisions of homeowners and individual actions of property owners and individual votes of town councils and individual bonds and rates approved by boards of supervisors weren't necessarily wrong. The big fire deals the same hand to everyone inside its perimeter.

She lived on Palmer, a block from Strawberry Drive, which lost twenty-five houses to the Garnet Fire. Thence it grew to twenty-nine, then nearly forty, and in the end burned forty-three civilian structures: thirty-two houses, six garages or sheds, and the barn where Heather Swanson kept her five miniature Shetlands. The fire was, in the end, contained, but it left a district of hill faces blackened, bereft. Pine Hollow had changed, and Tryon knew that it was his task to restore some sort of order, to set boundaries and make decisions. He needed information, and information depended on people: where they had been before the fire, how far they'd traveled during it; where they would be moving next.

Carla Diaz was the perfect informer. She was central, and also rooted, a source who'd already proven herself reliable to all relevant interests in the Pine Hollow exclusion zone: county and state authorities as well as the insurance companies. Carla owed money to everybody. During the evacuation, Rival Insurance had opened a special claims window on their website; she'd used the home office at JDM and sent an email to the general adjuster first thing Monday morning. She asked him to take a look at the house and set its value.

The next time would be different.

Almost everyone agrees that giant wildfires are an inevitable effect of climate change—we will just have to deal with them. But there is another way to look at the problem. The buildup of dry fuels in our forests is reversible. In fact the fuels that surrounded the Garnet Fire had been accumulating since the mid-1800s, when systematic fire suppression began turning small, frequent fires into the sporadic catastrophes we have today, and you can't say climate change caused that.

There is a way to keep our forests from becoming tinderboxes, and that way is fire. You can't prescribe burn in hot dry weather, but you can use chainsaws to manually thin. In 2015, five years of drought and rising temperatures finally caught up to the accumulated fuels around Butler's meadow, and the Ochoco National Forest lit a 1,000-acre fire in it, next to impassible cliffs. The fire put 60-foot-tall lodgepole torches against the sky every evening, a sight that could draw crowds.

The wilderness boundary and the trail crossed the fireline south of the meadow, a hundred yards apart, and from there you could see the black fire scar lining the forest's edge, stretching a mile up the river. Her family had started there in 1977. Calderóns. There were two boys and Carla and her older sister. And her mother, who came from Mexico alone at fifteen. She'd grown up near Monterrey on a ranch. Late morning, horses were pastured in the high meadows above the barn, and the air filled with dust when they moved in a herd. She was the horsekeeper's daughter, and every day she fed them and rode them in the pasture and helped put the rope snares on their necks for the roundup.

This was after the revolution, the first one, when the president ran from Mexico City to the US to keep from being killed. They grew lettuce and carrots and chard in the high ground and in the time between rains they worked on the house the horsekeeper was building out of wooden pallets.

She was married at sixteen then got pregnant almost at once. She had a son at seventeen, the year her own mother suddenly died. A man killed her on the road from Monterey to Saltillo, and her brothers came for her. Her daughter-in-law was there and saw the coffin sitting in the road.

The horsekeeper was a good man but his money ran out, so the new wife and her sisters and cousins rode into Guadalupe de la Trinidad and found empty homemade funeral homes to bury her in. After she stayed a few days the horsekeeper's son, the dead woman's brother, took a handgun and shot her husband. The pistol was small and weak, like a starter pistol, and the horsekeeper just got cut above his eye.

The Army came then for the dead man's son because they said he'd helped. All of his family came with him to the bus station, and everyone cried. By noon the air cleared, and some people stopped by the roadside to pick up hot stones and watch them cool on the soles of their shoes. Smoke wasn't the smell of fire, fire was the smell of smoke. Sandra Diaz walked back up the hill to her house two blocks over and stood in the driveway.

Everything flammable had burned: cable, cedar, garbage, utility poles, all of it charred on the ground. There wasn't much to amuse herself with, so she started walking. She came to the end of her garden and saw the grass had yellowed. She looked north, to the ridge, and how far it seemed. Her glowing garden limned a sequence in her mind, one to the next, days and days swinging round Plum River, the morning her daughter's engagement party had been canceled, the closet door pinned shut by a mirror, her cat upstairs in bed, and when the phone rang finally she pictured her daughter delivering the news and had the foresight to turn off the water because the pipes would have melted, and at that empty moment in the house filled with lost furniture and all the wildfires locked in the closet with her, the war approached.

*The operative word is "intended: No human or ecological community stands resolved – they can only ever be attempted. A human being, for instance, berths a spirit it's only partially aware of. The Fire Chief

At ten on Tuesday, the fifth day of the fire, Ralph Benjamin arrived at his station house on North Cedar Street. Seeing the charred houses on Horizon, his first instinct was that he wanted to stay inside. But he had a more than full-time job. People needed to believe that Pine Hollow and Area 1 were going to be rebuilt. Ralph had become the face of that effort, and whether it was false advertising or not, he was going to convince Pine Hollow it wasn't.

Buoyed by a cup of second coffee, he went out to the front lot and snapped on the earflap cap he'd inherited when the last chief retired, a gift from the previous assistant chief. It felt heavy today.

She'd gotten up earlier than she usually did on weekdays, ate breakfast on the back porch where she could watch the fir trees that once rippled beside her shed, and by seven she'd peeled down the dirt driveway with her moving boxes in the bed. In Crater Lake she'd found a Toyota dealer with a rental. By eight she was back at the lake for breakfast with some friends from her church. She'd all but forgotten about the fire last night when they got word that it was heading their way again. The town ordered its semiannual evacuation—another two thousand people, some of whom barely had time to get their keys before they had to spend the night in their cars. She covered the plates on her window with a towel and slept on the couch.

Those first four days, the fire had been on easy ground. It hadn't behaved any differently than it was supposed to. It had crept south in the chaparral; it had come down narrow canyons toward towns and stopped; it had spread through grassy meadows. Even in the Cottonwood Mountains—hot, rocky, and dry, with fifty-mile-an-hour winds—crews had been able to corral it by late afternoon, with bulldozers scraping containment lines in the dirt and water-dropping helicopters making lazy loops overhead. The fire was doing what it was supposed to do, until it got going in the southern part of the river canyon and reached the foot of the ridge, when it started doing what it wasn't supposed to.

Flames rolled all the way down the hill side—five, six hundred yards—leaving only gray trunks and singed branches behind.

On the way out, Carla had grabbed her mother's wallet and keys, a folder with her current insurance policy, and the house plan. Shawna Lunde drives four miles to work and four miles home in the same direction every day. Weather and forest type being roughly equal, traffic is the biggest factor shaping an incident commander's decisions. "It's one thing to come into a situation where it's an evacuation one way and your evacuation routes are safe and quick," Lunde says. "It's totally different if you have got two routes that are good, then all of a sudden you've got a fire that's causing closure, back-up, and reroute." Traffic means time, and time fixes pretty much everything. "Time is that ineffable thing that makes it all come together," says Danny Hoover, a wildland firefighter and author of the book Wildland Fire Today. "When we have plenty of time, we do good work. We like time. More time is always better."

If you asked Shawna Lunde for a history of the Garnet Fire, like you would ask a history professor, it would probably start on September 7, when it began as a dry lightning strike on a south-facing slope near the community of Tray Mountain, outside Sisters. Lightning sparked fourteen fires that day. About 200 firefighters came in to put them out, and all but the Garnet were contained that first day.

Within two days the fire had doubled in size. On the fourth day it jumped into the forests around Pine Hollow. On the fifth day it ran close to populated areas, about 60 percent of which were evacuated. About ten days after it started, the fire consumed a historic lookout which had been built in 1926, and a hundred yards farther on it reached Pine Hollow Drive. There was some fire to the east and some to the west. If it unified, with the wind behind it, there isn't much anyone could do to stop it from burning through the town.

Fifteen miles away, in Roanoke, Ivan Vogel III posted photos of the fire to the Elko County Facebook page.

Vogel was the county manager. He'd helped found the emergency management office in 1977, and he was the first county manager to put public affairs in the job description. When he retired in 2018, after nearly forty years, he kept a desk.

Vogel had moved his own mother to safety that first morning. On the Facebook page, he'd kept posting about evacuation centers and road closures for twelve hours. In the fall of the previous year, there were more than ten million acres of short-rotation poplar plantations in the United States. Unlike open fields and fields that look open but aren't—they are fields of waving grain, or fields of cumin, or fields of different grasses, some wild and some mown and some only half covered by weeds, like somebody forgot to stitch them up right—poplar tree fields look like fields. This is why people turn them into fields.

It's a transformation that happens in four steps: destroy, plant, cut, destroy. First, the local ecosystem is destroyed. This can be done by heavy machinery or by about as much horsepower as you can get under your feet. Farmers running tractors have fewer problems with rocks and burrowing insects than those driving goats or cattle. Farmers driving bulldozers do even better, although ground cover can get caught on their blades. There is debate on whether wildfire would be worse for leading the clear, or whether it would encourage weeds and brush.

Once all surface obstacles have been removed, poplar trees may be planted. These are generally large, balled nursery varieties that cost more but have a higher survival rate, even on flattened terrain. Unlike most large, coniferous trees—which have long taproots to get water, and grow straight so that sunlight can reach the upper leaves, and have seeds that live in tight cones that open when their temperature falls, making sure they grow in an area where the parent plant will be of no help in raising them—poplars are wild places. Pop lars propogate by riverbanks that crumble with the current. In the spring thousands of them can bristle along a curve of dirt in a single brown blur. Their roots go wide, not deep, and they grow fast not from a russet-clad pine cone, but by a naked quickening, and the breeze alone can round their growth patterns. In good soil the only thing stopping a clone from spreading around the world is time.

First she retrieved what was left of her house across the street, a burned trunk and a flue pipe, and came back across the lawn to put them with her mother's things. When she straightened, the excruciating sensation that had been building since she'd seen the first flames exploding over the ridge sent her to her knees. Smoke from the fire bit her clothes, a smell she would dream about for years. When she stood again, the sack with her mother's rings sloshed at her feet.

Her mother would teach copse and low scrub and red fir to her grandchildren. She would teach them aspen and pineapple and orange lucerne and teach them that you could make a living with your hands.

If you could get the fuck fire out of your county.

In a year Malaya rented an apartment in Sacramento and gave birth to a son in a hospital running on backup generators so the trucks could go fight more wildfires. She didn't want to give him up, but there just wasn't any money in firefighting anymore, and she needed health insurance. She named the baby Hugo, spelled the same as her father's name but with her mother's name.

"You have nothing to fear except fear itself," Malaya told Hugo. She knew her mother had been something of a divine creature. She gave all her time to helping people and never needed fear or anger as a source of energy. It was her favorite letter of advice, and now it occurred to her that Franklin Delano Roosevelt hadn't been her mom. "Tell me how the mighty have fallen," she said to her son in a sing–song voice. Hugo blinked his eyes. Malaya said to him, "I don't know, son, I don't know."

The last house on the left at the foot of the street was also destroyed—collapse of the roof, gutted second floor, brittle black ash on everything. Carla slowed her car at each one and looked across the street at her own house. The predominant color was still beige. The fence was still up, the Coors sign in the yard still readable. Broken windows and burnt siding stood out incongruously against the rest, and even so, the house looked like it could still house a family. Like no one would hound you out of it with a bullhorn screaming, "Mandatory evacuation in effect!"

She killed the engine, got out, and stood holding the heat of the day against her grief. Then she checked her phone and started for the foot of Maple Street. She wasn't sure why. Maybe to see if she could find the neighbor's cat, or to see whether her mother's maple tree was still alive.

Pine needles carpeted the sidewalk and gutter, and the queen Anne's lace that usually grew by the curb looked charred and lifeless. Parts of curb and gutter had liquefied in the heat. Only the flagstones of the drive at Number 9 had held the fire's heat, not enough to scorch the blue spruce there, although their white bark looked parched and peeled.

At the corner she turned and looked back at her own house, or what was left of it. Even from here she could see the black vee over the living room windows where the window coverings had hung. Next door at Number 5 a woman was walking down her blackened front steps.

"Hi," Carla called. "Any sign of a cat?"

The woman shook her head and hugged herself. "Not yet." She squinted past Carla at the empty lot at Number 6. "Hey," she said, "what's left of your place—maybe I can move my stuff over there, put a tarp, keep the rain off."

Carla had no answer. If the woman was heading for what was left of her house, maybe she was a friend, or a caseworker, or someone sent from the Red Cross. She just nodded and kept walking to the end of the block. At the remains of Number 3 she found the charred lump of what might have been

was still standing. Some houses on the street already had red tags on their doors; the rest had no markers at all. She parked by the curb, got out, and breathed in the air. It stung her nose and made her eyes water, but it was air.

She picked her way along the sidewalks, avoiding blackened boards and scorched step-skids and patches of ash. An ember caught in the leaves beside the library and flickered out. The house next door was gone. Hers was still there.

She pulled her phone from her pocket and walked up the charred front walk. It had been painted blue once, years and years ago, but the fire had burned it to the natural wood. She snapped a photo and sent it with a text: This the one?

The reply came quickly: Yes, that's it. I'll see you soon.

She left the porch and stood on the sidewalk and looked down the street. The smoke was lighter now, yellowish, and as she watched it thin to a haze and then dissolve. Nothing about the fire had been anyone's fault, except maybe the deputy who'd let everyone back in too soon—even that was maybe—but everything that happened afterward belonged to the people who lived there. She texted her mother: I'm coming back.

She started to walk back to the car and then stopped, fished the photo of her mother out of her pocket, and held it up before her face. She stood for a long time in the shade of the burned walkway and looked at the face in the photo and the face before her and tried to see her mother in them both. Then she let herself keep walking and her mother, eighteen months sober now, hiked up the street behind her.

Nate Granville was trying to get into his house three doors up, in a standoff with a firefighter in turnout pants. "Permission to enter?" Nate asked him.

The firefighter studied his clipboard. "Do you own this place?"

Nate nodded.

"House number?"

"Four-nineteen. Highlights overlook the pond, if you want the description, scallywag."

The firefighter marked the clipboard and stepped back. "Fire's headed northeast. Probably hit this street in less than an hour. If your name is on the ownership, you can go in."

Nate didn't wait. He seemed disappointed somehow, and when he pushed open his front door and bounded inside, Carla heard him call, "Maya? Sky? It's Papa!"

She walked up her own porch steps, holding her breath, and saw that the family room window on the far side was open—and the curtain was waving in the wind. The threshold was cool when she stepped inside.

She said, " Mom? It's me."

Only the fridge hummed. She opened the kitchen door. Sunlight poured in through a screen of black leaves. The table was still set from breakfast. Carla heard her mother's voice from down the hallway, thin and faint. "Carla? Is that you?"

She followed it to the bedroom, but her mother was not there. She was in the bathroom, kneeling on the floor, opening the medicine cabinet. She was gray around the edges, wrung out and shrunken since the night before. But she was there. Her mother.

Carla knelt beside her. "Hi, Mom," she said. "We made it back."

Her mother was crying. "I felt the heat," she said. "I thought—"

Carla took her mother's shoulder in her hand. "I know. It's okay. We're okay. We're home."

was gone. Not just gone, but leveled, with nothing behind it but the blackened remains of pine trees falling away into the hillside. (Apologies in advance to readers who have lived this reality.) Across the street the church had burned partly to the ground. The store, where Carla had begged for a puppy on her eighth birthday, was just a burned shell. The only building that still had color and any kind of shape was the school. It still stood upright. 

To the east, the fire had burned slowly up the length of the street. Everything was black on that side—houses, landscaping, lawns—except the parts that had already burned last year. Her mother's garden, where she'd grown petunias and zinnias every spring and summer for thirty years, was nothing but charred stumps. 

Carla got out and sat on the curb, looking, while the light turned from slate-gray to red and then faded again. After half an hour, Ken Travers, the county fire marshal, pulled up and parked. He told her that four firefighters had tangled with the edge of the fire when it crested the ridge at about 2 A.M. Someone called it in, but by the time a plane and a helitanker got overhead the spot fire had already gotten going and had spread halfway down the street.

"That's where they made their stand," Ken said. "They saved the school, anyhow."

He took her to what was left of the Diaz house, stood around with her for a while, and told her that the investigation would take a while but that it was definitely arson. He handed her a card for Pine Creek Mental Health. Carla thanked him, and when he left she sat on the curb a while longer. On the busted foundation of what had been her family home she felt adrift and hollow. She put her head on her knees, trying not to let the sobbing start, and texted her best friend, Dana, who had evacuated with her parents to a hotel in Redding. USED TO LIVE THERE, she typed. Up on the ridge someone had built a lookout with folding chairs and a windsock. Carla drove up and parked. She took off her windbreaker and spread it on the folding chair. The wind was blowing east, as forecast, but the fire didn't look contained. She could see heat rolling up from several different parts of the burn area. As she watched, a spot fire ignited farther down the ridge. It burned for 20 minutes and then slowly died out, making no headway against the wind. Directly below her a tip fire crept through the unburned edge of the forest, climbing up the front of a ridge only to burn out a few yards later. She picked up her phone and began recording.

Half an hour later a fire_info account tweeted that the fire had moved into "the heart of the subdivision." Carla sighed and put away the phone. Although she hadn't seen flames, the spot fires meant the crowns of the trees—where the fire could race through the canopy—were still burning, and as the fire moved farther into the unburned shade, it could run again. Spot fires meant the embers were still traveling ahead of the main burn.

Someone came up and sat next to her. He was seventyish and wearing a Pine Hollow T-shirt and bandanna. Carla asked if he lived nearby. He said he used to, but that his house was gone.

There was a powdery gray coating on her mother's mailbox and a heap of ash in the gutter edged with the flayed and smoldering skin of a possum. The house next door still stood, but everything around it was blackened and seemed shrunken, and the clothesline drooped with nothing but a few dead leaves.

At Carla's own house the playground equipment in the cul-de-sac was still recognizable but blackened, and an acrid rain had left wet spots on the picnic tables. The houses near the school were streaked with soot as if they'd been cut with giant sooty razors. Where the fire had been hottest the whole block was stripped to pavement. She found her old bikes where they'd fallen, warped, the tires run flat. She thought she'd feel something terrible, but mostly what she felt was relief—to be back, to have made a choice, to be finished with the worry.

A group of firefighters was gathered at the school field, sitting on their trucks, drinking from paper cups. Carla stopped in front of them and asked what had happened. One of the men wiped his mouth with the back of his hand and said, "It jumped the ridge around ten last night and hit this block hard. Didn't leave much, but people got out OK."

She told him where her mother had gone and asked if he'd seen the woman who'd been her neighbor for thirty years, a tiny woman who always wore slippers no matter how far she walked. He shook his head.

Carla went to the remains of her own house and began picking through the debris, deciding what to keep. Her first instinct was to take only things that were useful or dear, but that felt wrong. When she picked up her mother's address book she felt dizzy, as if she'd been pulled out of the water and was trying to remember what to breathe. She sat on the ligneous ruins of a dining-room chair and sorted.

Even though the light was hopeful and the smoke overhead was beginning to thin, she knew that her life was over as it had been—broken cleanly at the moment the fire had jumped the ridge, the way a stick is cleanly broken by a fall. As she came closer she could see that the back porch disagreed with the front: charred and black, but standing. She went around back in case the fire had jumped over from the neighbor's. The rosemary was gone and in its place the stone path was gone too; it was just a smoking depression in the ground. But the conduits for her fairy lights were intact, and even the lights themselves seemed to be mostly in one piece. She was so surprised she laughed out loud. Then she saw that the fire had gone around the outside of the house and was still smoldering in the woodpile along the side of the garage.

She took off her sweater and beat the larger pieces into embers. She worked from back to front and didn't stop until her mother came around the corner with a damp dish towel, looking worried.

"It's out," Carla said. "I think."

Her mother stepped onto the porch and inhaled, looking at the unburned roses on the west side. "Then why does it smell like a chimney?"

They went inside and closed the door. The living room smelled the same, so did the kitchen. But the smoke sorted itself out, rising and moving up and out the way it was supposed to. After an hour Carla made coffee and they sat at the table on the back deck and did inventory. The lily beds had burned—the other side of the street, the Spencers said later, so hadn't theirs? The Hyacinths were fine.

"I'm Carla," she said, and realized she didn't know his name. He introduced himself, and even though it was far too late for a first meeting, she liked the look of him, the way he wasn't shy about walking up to a stranger in distress and offering help.

"How close did it get?" she asked.

He pointed down the street. "To about there, maybe less." The neighbor had been sitting in his front yard, so his estimate was approximate. "I ran a line to the hydrant," he said. He had a telephone lineman's build and the sunburn of a man not used to shirts. "We should get a decent stream going."

They let water splash over the roof for a while. Carla put the nozzle in her hand and sprayed the firebreak her mother had dug along the edge of the yard, the old money she'd hated but now, seeing what the fire could do, found herself grateful for.

The neighbor glanced at the open back door of her mother's house and said, "She went in?"

Carla nodded. "About midnight, I think. She couldn't stand to stay away any longer."

"That makes sense." He looked up the street again. "You're lucky. Might be your whole street made it."

By then the Garnet Fire had been burning for four days in the national forest west of town, and it was three miles out, on the far side of Sawyer Ridge. Pine Hollow had about six hundred homes, a K–8 school, and one road out. Carla's own house was two blocks over Aspen Street, where ten years earlier she'd limped home from the gradeschool soccer field after her knee buckled mid-play and stayed in the house for a week while her mother fretted over her.

Everything depended on the wind. The forecast called for it to swing around to the east overnight, but Carla had heard the fire crew forecasting around the coffee pots for a southwesterly shift, which would drive the Garnet Fire over Sawyer Ridge and down toward them. If that happened, there wouldn't be much anyone could do to stop it.

They spent the night at the fairgrounds in Delton, the seat of the neighboring township, on cots in the livestock barn with two hundred other townspeople. Nobody slept much. People kept checking their phones, but the fire maps weren't updating. The radio only said crews were "engaged." Carla spent the night lying next to her mother, who held the photo album she'd grabbed off the shelf in her hurry.When the sheriff's office announced, around seven a.m., that residents could drive back in as far as the turnoff for Aspen Street, Carla left her mother with a neighbor and took her own car. PAUL TSOEVER IS A FIREman.

He was twenty-six and lived with his parents in Ute City, forty minutes east of Pine Hollow. In August, when he wasn't on call with the select crew, he laid pavers for fourteen dollars an hour.

Paul was not one for hoarding feelings. He texted when he was happy and when he was sad and when he felt dutiful. His texts were brief and straightforward. "Hey," "Take care," "It sucks." If he was in town and someone called him for help, he would take a break from whatever he was doing and come.

Doing the right thing was important to Paul. He knew it wasn't always simple. When he was eighteen he, accidentally, badly, got a girl pregnant and did the honorable thing, as his mother had always defined it: He married her, even though he didn't love her, and after the baby came they lived together for two years. Then he'd asked her what she wanted, and she'd said she wanted him to go. So he'd gone, taking only a duffle bag and the baby and the squirrel cage with the transport cage inside that his father had made for him. He'd left the rest — the tuba he couldn't fit in the car, the tile saw, the wedding ring on the dresser — and he'd not looked back.

That marriage and its ending left Paul with a clear idea of what he owed other people and what he could and could not give. He knew he was a good firefighter. He'd begun as a seasonal the summer after high school, when he was nineteen. At first he'd been angry at everything — the condescension of the crew leaders, the lingo, the work, the long, smoky days. Then, gradually, things made sense to him. Paul liked systems. He liked the way an impact wrench could be used to tighten a bolt until it would strip, but in a fire it could also break a hydrant coupling if you set it on the right setting. He liked the way a forklift could carry half a ton of hose up a flight of stairs if you balanced it correctly and didn't go too fast. He liked rules that let you work fast and made things come out right. Fire was the ultimate system: unthinking, merciless, physics given free rein

Your job is to get the reader interested at the beginning and not lose them. A story about a fire whose direction depends on the forecast? Lots of cliches, even potentially trite. But the specifics here make it come alive, and the narrator is engaging in a direct way, sharing something personal, attitudes and emotions and history. This is not a news report: it's an experience, and by the end you're asking yourself, what will happen to Aspen Street? to Carla and her mother?

The one thing you can say about a certification program and an MFA is that they teach you, again and again, not to do this:

Exposition is eventdata in disguise. My mother and I were two of the six hundred residents of Pine Hollow, incorporated in 1947 and annexed by the town of Pineville ten years later. "Exposition" is the tradatorium's word for material that is only there to provide information, like a story opening with the sentence, "When Harry walked into the diner that rainy night, little did he know that his life would never be the same." Someone made a fortune selling T-shirts that said, "STORY STATEMENT? THERE IS NO FRIGGING STORY STATEMENT." And yet we find them everywhere, because writers are human and lazy. Lazy even enough not to notice that a sentence that starts "When I was seven" is nothing but a story statement in disguise.

So. How do you avoid this? Interestingly, the very thing that balances the opening of the Carla Diaz story is a kind of exposition, but it's disguised as something else. Notice that after the narrative opening, we get this line: "Everything depended on the wind." That's exposition, of course, but it's also atmosphere, mood, theme. In short, it's doing several things at once. It's also a good example of deep vs. surface detail. The first part of the story is full of surface detail: the time management of the evacuation, the description of the fairgrounds, the neighbor Carla finds for her mother, the aspects of the physical world, what she can see from the car, and so forth. But "Everything depended on the wind" is deep, thematic detail, an abstract, even philosophical idea made concrete.

I've been thinking about Carla, and people like her whom I've never met, since our own valley burned last summer. When my husband and I moved to a town just south of Missoula, Mont., the plan was to tuck ourselves in as a buffer zone between a working forest and the borders of the city. Our house shares a driveway with three others, with meadows on one side and forest on the other, often visited by deer, bears, bobcats, and mountain lions. Just down the road is a working mill, where our neighbor cuts beams for new houses as well as saps for making longbows. But what is a home? It's not a raft that can be pulled out to sea.
We're on the edge of a killing zone.

For nearly a week this summer, we were one of many towns threatened by Montana's Hamby Fire. From my open porch I watched what began as a controlled burn at Glacier National Park barbecue itself out of control and through the vast, dry forests of northwestern Montana, swallowing cabins, vacation homes, and holding places. Carbon Worley, a single-room schoolhouse built in 1915, was burned to the ground. Homes in every town north of here were evacuated, including Meadowlark, a forest neighborhood five miles down Interstate 90 from our house, where I put my mother-in-law to sleep when she's tired. Trotter Meadow was burned in one flare; it's a beautiful meadow that most Missoulians have visited. Lilac Park was burned; so were the old cabinets in the basement, which people use for storing family keepsakes. Any hope that our university-run paper mill might become a source for biofuels was burned to cinders.

The fire then turned and marched into the Bob Marshall Wilderness, where my cousin and I caught trout as children and where great grizzly bears live—and, it seems most likely from here, will die, as there's nowhere left for them to go.

At last the moon and the clouds turned green, and the air smelled like pitch. Near my home a skeleton of lodge pole pine was blown down, pointed for the road. Even now I'm scared of a breeze.
